title: Subhuti weeps (section 14)
hook: hearing it, Subhuti weeps; the Buddha recalls being cut apart by a king without anger, because he had no idea of a self

segments.voice: Yesterday, the diamond's name: the sutra names itself, then cuts the name. Your line: the diamond cuts. Which label did you use without letting it close around you? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-one.

So far in this sutra, Subhuti has been the steady one. Calm, exact, the student with the careful answer every time. The Buddha has praised him for dwelling in peace. Then, at the start of section fourteen, the text says he hears this teaching and understands its meaning deeply, and he weeps. Tears, from the one praised for his peace. And then he speaks through them, and the Buddha answers with a memory from very long ago. Today: Subhuti weeps.
screen: `THE STEADY ONE.` → `HE UNDERSTANDS, AND WEEPS.` → `A MEMORY FROM LONG AGO.`

segments.voice: First, the tears. Subhuti says that since he gained the eye of wisdom, he has never heard a teaching like this one. Someone who hears it with a clear, trusting mind, he says, will see things as they truly are, and that is rare and wonderful. Second, rare in a later age. He's been taught directly, so trusting it is not hard for him, he says. But someone in a later time who hears this and trusts it will be rare. The Buddha agrees, and adds: anyone who hears this and isn't startled, isn't frightened, isn't afraid, is rare indeed. Third, the memory. Long ago, the Buddha says, a king cut his body apart, limb from limb. And at that time he had no idea of a self, a person, a being, a life. If he had held such an idea, he says, anger and ill will would have risen in him. They didn't. He calls this the perfection of patience, and then, in the sutra's way, says it is not the perfection of patience. Fourth, why the tears? The sutra doesn't explain them. Some readers hear joy, the relief of finally hearing it said. Some hear grief for how long it took. Some hear both. The text simply lets him weep, and keeps going. And the memory beside the tears is not a lesson in pretending a wound doesn't hurt. It's a claim about where anger comes from: from the idea of a self that has been wronged. That's an extreme story, told about a Buddha. Everyday hurts are smaller. A remark. A slight at work. The same question can still be asked of them, gently.
screen: `SUBHUTI WEEPS.` · `RARE: NOT STARTLED, NOT AFRAID.` · `CUT APART, WITHOUT ANGER.` · `WHY THE TEARS? THE TEXT DOESN'T SAY.` · then, large: `HE WEPT TO HEAR IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: soften toward one hurt. Not the biggest one. A small one, from this week or this month. Settle, and breathe. Let it come to mind, and notice where the body holds it: the jaw, the chest, the shoulders. Breathe into that place. You don't have to excuse what happened, or decide it was fine. Just notice the one inside who was hurt, and the story that keeps telling it. Let the grip ease, one breath's worth. If it doesn't, that's all right. Come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Subhuti weeps. Hearing the sutra and understanding it deeply, Subhuti weeps; the Buddha recalls being cut apart without anger, because he held no idea of a self. Today's word.
Your line: he wept to hear it. Today, when something true moves you, let it, without explaining it away. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhists count patience among the perfections of a bodhisattva, and teachers tell the story of the sage of patience and the king alongside this section.

pairs: no idea of a self, so no anger
is not the perfection of patience

myth: the sutra explains exactly why Subhuti weeps
it doesn't. readers hear joy, grief, or both; the text lets him weep.
the Buddha says anger would have arisen if he'd held an idea of a self
he had no such idea, and so no anger or ill will.
Subhuti says this teaching is easy for anyone to trust
trusting it is not hard for him, he says, but one who trusts it in a later age will be rare. the Buddha adds that whoever isn't startled or afraid is rare indeed.

fork.setup: you're the sage in the Buddha's memory. a king is cutting your body apart. what does the story say happened in your mind?
options: anger, held back by sheer willpower.
no idea of a self, and so no anger.
fork.reveal: he had no idea of a self, a person, a being or a life. if he had, the Buddha says, anger and ill will would have arisen.

original.note: Sanskrit: patience, forbearance; the perfection the Buddha names in this section.

trapdoor: what you thought: patience means gritting your teeth and holding the anger in.
what it means: in the Buddha's memory, there was no anger to hold in, because there was no idea of a self being wronged.
what a scholar hears: kshanti, the perfection of patience, given the sutra's treatment: named, then said not to be the perfection of patience, so it isn't held as an achievement.

notes: Section numbering follows the common 32-section division of Kumarajiva's Chinese text.
All wording paraphrased (quoted: null). The king is left unnamed: Kumarajiva has King Kali (歌利王), and some English versions say the king of Kalinga; a Keeper can decide whether to name him.
The sutra's 'last five hundred years' and the sage of patience's 'five hundred lifetimes' are left out under the claims rule.
The readings of the tears (joy, grief, both) are offered as 'some readers'; confirm they are fair to the commentaries.

Editor pass: attribution fixed. In Kumarajiva's text Subhuti says a later hearer who trusts the sutra will be rare; it is the Buddha who says one who is not startled, frightened or afraid is rare indeed. The teach and a myth reveal now say so, and the match pair is relabeled. Cut 'that's why it's called so' after the perfection of patience, since Kumarajiva's line there has no 'that is why it is called' clause (check other versions). Replaced the stock 'on an ordinary Tuesday'.
